The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. # Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

Here is my invention.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

3	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. 4	
5	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.

7	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. 10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

1	<!-- Detailed Description - body text only, no heading line. -->
2	
3	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
4	
5	Overview
6	
7	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.
8	
9	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
10	
11	The base
12	
13	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
14	
15	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
16	
17	The vibration motor
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
20	
21	The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
26	
27	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
28	
29	The perimeter member and the chamber
30	
31	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.
34	
35	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
36	
37	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
38	
39	The pressure differential that holds the device down
40	
41	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
42	
43	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
44	
45	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
46	
47	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
48	
49	The vibration transmission path
50	
51	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
52	
53	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
54	
55	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside that contact, being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating the bearing face 26 from the exposed face 38 everywhere: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
56	
57	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
58	
59	Handles
60	
61	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
62	
63	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
64	
65	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
66	
67	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
68	
69	Method of use
70	
71	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
72

In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside that contact, being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating the bearing face 26 from the exposed face 38 everywhere: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

content.text: I've read the disclosure, the full conversation, all nine draft sections, `draft/numerals.md`, and all five figure briefs. Here is the complete ledger review.

input.summary: Ledger built against the single inventor source (disclosure.md, reproduced verbatim in the one substantive USER turn of conversation.md; every later USER turn is a resume/repair/corrective instruction and gives no new technical support). The nine sections are unusually disciplined: the claim set (18 claims, 3 independents), the numeral table (16 entries, each used exactly once and each appearing on at least one sheet), the Brief Description, and the Detailed Description trace cleanly to the disclosure for the base/first side/second side, motor coupling, air-extraction mechanism and vacuum-pump species, chamber, rigid loop-or-skirt perimeter, the plastic/metal/PTFE/combination-of-rigid-materials list, the not-a-seal + restricted-inflow + sub-atmospheric chamber mechanism, the operator-free holding force, the rigid undamped transmission path, sliding to successive areas, handles for guiding, and the rope/wire/cable pulling element with decoupled control. No drafting note, placeholder, bracketed request, open question, or unresolved alternative remains in the patent text, and claim/description terminology is uniform. The defects found are (i) two places where the description states clearance geometry and clearance magnitude as fact where the disclosure states neither, (ii) an absolute "operator applies no downward force / hands carry no part of the load" that overshoots the disclosure's "without requiring the operator to press downward," (iii) several invented shapes and proportions in the figure briefs (rectangular housings and their spacing, base overhang, even-thickness slab, rectangular loop), (iv) a handle depicted on the pulling-element embodiment that the disclosure presents as an alternative, (v) one claim-to-description condition mismatch on continuous extraction, (vi) one Brief-Description-to-brief omission mismatch on FIG. 2, and (vii) residual process scaffolding in numerals.md. No rendered image was inspected.

findings.title: Clearance magnitude asserted as fact ("far too small to be drawn to scale") with no source passage on clearance size
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md, "The perimeter member and the chamber", paragraph beginning "Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal"; figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md, Geometry to be drawn
findings.detail: The description states a dimensional fact about the invention: that the clearance is so small it cannot be drawn to scale, and that FIG. 4 draws it "many times its true height." The disclosure never gives any dimension, magnitude, ratio, or order of size for the gap beneath the perimeter. It says only that the perimeter is not intended to seal and that it restricts airflow. "Restricts airflow" does not affirmatively establish any true height, nor that the true height is below drawable scale. There is no affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER turn stating a clearance dimension; the nearest source wording is the qualitative "it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile." The figure brief inherits the same unsourced premise by specifying a "tall open space" whose existence at that proportion depends on the invented smallness of the real gap.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile." No affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER message states the size of the clearance.
findings.fix: In draft/07-detailed-description.md replace the two quoted sentences with: "The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4." In figures/FIG-4 change "Because the view is greatly enlarged, the gap between the column and the upper band is a tall open space, the bottom line of the column standing well above the unbroken top edge line of the upper band." to "The gap between the column and the upper band is shown as an open space, the bottom line of the column standing above the unbroken top edge line of the upper band, so that the clearance is clearly visible."

findings.title: Exclusive clearance-here / contact-everywhere-else geometry stated as fact in the description
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md, "The vibration transmission path", paragraph beginning "The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop"
findings.detail: The description asserts a definite spatial partition of the bearing interface: clearance along part of the loop only, hard direct contact over "the remainder" of the loop, with the vibration carried by that contact and not by the clearance. The disclosure affirms two things separately - that air enters beneath the rigid perimeter, and that the perimeter maintains rigid contact with the tile - but it nowhere describes where the clearance lies, that it is confined to part of the loop, that contact subsists over the balance of the loop, or that vibration crosses at the contact rather than at the gap. The broad claim recital "along at least part of the perimeter member" is the acceptable, non-exclusive reading and can stand; the description's exclusive version ('only along part ... rather than ... everywhere') is the untraced addition and is what a reader would treat as a described structural requirement.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside that contact, being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating the bearing face 26 from the exposed face 38 everywhere." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter." No affirmative passage states that the clearance occupies only part of the perimeter or that contact subsists over the remainder.
findings.fix: Replace the two quoted sentences with: "Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member." This keeps literal support for the "along at least part" recital in claims 1, 10 and 14 without asserting an unsourced partition of the interface.

findings.title: Absolute "no downward force is applied by an operator" exceeds the disclosure's "without requiring the operator to press downward"
findings.where: draft/08-claims.md claim 17; draft/07-detailed-description.md "The pressure differential that holds the device down" ("In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.") and "The force balance ..." ("the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force", "Because the operator applies no downward force"); draft/05-summary.md paragraph beginning "Two consequences follow"; draft/09-abstract.md
findings.detail: The disclosure states that the pressure differential holds the device without requiring operator downward pressure, and that operator pressure and fatigue are minimized. The candidate converts a permissive statement (the operator need not press) into an absolute factual and claimed condition (the operator applies none, hands carry no part of the contact load). No affirmative passage says the operator in fact applies zero downward force or that the hands carry none of the contact load; the disclosure's own summary sentence speaks of 'minimizing' pressure, not eliminating it. Claim 17 recites the absolute as a positive method limitation, so the mismatch is a scope defect as well as a fidelity one. Claims 5 and 13 are correctly drafted ('sufficient to hold ... without a downward force being applied') and should be the model.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 17): "wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein no downward force is applied to the vibration device by an operator while the vibration motor operates." Candidate (description): "In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load." Source (disclosure.md): "The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward." and "The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator." No passage states that no downward force is applied.
findings.fix: Claim 17: replace the second clause with "and wherein the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element without a downward force being required from the operator." Description: replace "In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load." with "The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands."; replace "Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path" with "Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained"; replace "the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer" with "the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer". Abstract: change "without downward force from the operator" to "without downward force being required from the operator"; Summary: change "the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped" to "the operator need not press the device against the covering element, so the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped".

findings.title: Invented housing shapes, housing spacing and base overhang in the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs
findings.where: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md, Geometry to be drawn (base 12, vibration motor 18, air-extraction mechanism 20, handle 44); figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md, Geometry to be drawn (vibration device 10)
findings.detail: The briefs specify shapes, proportions and spatial relationships that no source passage supplies: that the motor and the air-extraction mechanism are each a rectangular housing, that the two housings do not touch, that the motor is the left-hand housing, that the base is a flat slab that runs past both housings at both ends so that its top face is exposed beyond them, and that the handle stands clear of the two housings. The disclosure says only that the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are each coupled to the first side of a rigid base, and that the device may include one or more handles. The overhang requirement in particular is an invented proportion of exactly the class the standing corrective USER message identified for removal ('remove invented exact counts and proportions not grounded in the disclosure'); it exists to create a labelling target rather than to depict a disclosed structure.
findings.evidence: Candidate (FIG. 1): "The base 12 is the flat slab that carries the other bodies, the only slab on the sheet, running past them at both ends, so that its top face is exposed beyond them." and "The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular housing standing on the top face of the base 12, drawn as the left-hand of the two housings" and "The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a rectangular housing ... the two housings not touching." Source (disclosure.md): "The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side." No affirmative passage gives any housing shape, relative position, separation, or base overhang.
findings.fix: In both briefs, recast these as depiction conventions rather than asserted structure: "The base 12 is the slab that carries the other bodies, the only slab on the sheet; its top face remains visible where no body stands on it. Identified well inside the visible part of its top face, clear of every bounding line." and "The vibration motor 18 is one of the two bodies carried on the top face of the base 12, shown as a simple housing, with no body in front of it. Identified well inside its front face." and "The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the other body carried on the top face of the base 12, shown as a separate simple housing. Identified well inside its front face." Apply the same wording to the corresponding sentence in the FIG. 5 brief ("the base, shown as a slab, and two separate simple housings carried on it").

findings.title: FIG. 2 brief specifies a base of even thickness, which the disclosure does not state
findings.where: figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-CHAMBER.md, Geometry to be drawn ("The base 12 is of even thickness and is hatched throughout." and the bullet "The base 12 is the horizontal hatched slab, of even thickness.")
findings.detail: Even thickness is a specific sectional proportion of the base. The disclosure describes the base only as rigid, with a first side and a second side; the detailed description likewise defines rigidity functionally and says nothing about uniform thickness. Nothing in any USER passage affirms a constant-section base.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The base 12 is of even thickness and is hatched throughout." Source (disclosure.md): "a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base" - the only description of the base. No affirmative passage addresses its thickness or section.
findings.fix: Delete "of even thickness" from both sentences in the FIG. 2 brief, leaving "The base 12 is hatched throughout." and "The base 12 is the horizontal hatched slab. Identified well inside its hatching, clear of every bounding line."

findings.title: Rectangular plan shape of the perimeter loop is invented across FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5
findings.where: figures/FIG-3-BOTTOM-PLAN-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE.md ("two nested rectangles", "outermost rectangle", "innermost rectangle", "spaced apart on all four sides"); figures/FIG-1 and figures/FIG-5 ("a shallow rectangular band")

data.summary: Ledger built against the single inventor source (disclosure.md, reproduced verbatim in the one substantive USER turn of conversation.md; every later USER turn is a resume/repair/corrective instruction and gives no new technical support). The nine sections are unusually disciplined: the claim set (18 claims, 3 independents), the numeral table (16 entries, each used exactly once and each appearing on at least one sheet), the Brief Description, and the Detailed Description trace cleanly to the disclosure for the base/first side/second side, motor coupling, air-extraction mechanism and vacuum-pump species, chamber, rigid loop-or-skirt perimeter, the plastic/metal/PTFE/combination-of-rigid-materials list, the not-a-seal + restricted-inflow + sub-atmospheric chamber mechanism, the operator-free holding force, the rigid undamped transmission path, sliding to successive areas, handles for guiding, and the rope/wire/cable pulling element with decoupled control. No drafting note, placeholder, bracketed request, open question, or unresolved alternative remains in the patent text, and claim/description terminology is uniform. The defects found are (i) two places where the description states clearance geometry and clearance magnitude as fact where the disclosure states neither, (ii) an absolute "operator applies no downward force / hands carry no part of the load" that overshoots the disclosure's "without requiring the operator to press downward," (iii) several invented shapes and proportions in the figure briefs (rectangular housings and their spacing, base overhang, even-thickness slab, rectangular loop), (iv) a handle depicted on the pulling-element embodiment that the disclosure presents as an alternative, (v) one claim-to-description condition mismatch on continuous extraction, (vi) one Brief-Description-to-brief omission mismatch on FIG. 2, and (vii) residual process scaffolding in numerals.md. No rendered image was inspected.

findings.title: Clearance magnitude asserted as fact ("far too small to be drawn to scale") with no source passage on clearance size
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md, "The perimeter member and the chamber", paragraph beginning "Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal"; figures/FIG-4-ENLARGED-SECTION-OF-THE-PERIMETER-MEMBER-END.md, Geometry to be drawn
findings.detail: The description states a dimensional fact about the invention: that the clearance is so small it cannot be drawn to scale, and that FIG. 4 draws it "many times its true height." The disclosure never gives any dimension, magnitude, ratio, or order of size for the gap beneath the perimeter. It says only that the perimeter is not intended to seal and that it restricts airflow. "Restricts airflow" does not affirmatively establish any true height, nor that the true height is below drawable scale. There is no affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER turn stating a clearance dimension; the nearest source wording is the qualitative "it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile." The figure brief inherits the same unsourced premise by specifying a "tall open space" whose existence at that proportion depends on the invented smallness of the real gap.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile." No affirmative passage in the disclosure or in any USER message states the size of the clearance.
findings.fix: In draft/07-detailed-description.md replace the two quoted sentences with: "The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 is shown in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4." In figures/FIG-4 change "Because the view is greatly enlarged, the gap between the column and the upper band is a tall open space, the bottom line of the column standing well above the unbroken top edge line of the upper band." to "The gap between the column and the upper band is shown as an open space, the bottom line of the column standing above the unbroken top edge line of the upper band, so that the clearance is clearly visible."

findings.title: Exclusive clearance-here / contact-everywhere-else geometry stated as fact in the description
findings.where: draft/07-detailed-description.md, "The vibration transmission path", paragraph beginning "The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop"
findings.detail: The description asserts a definite spatial partition of the bearing interface: clearance along part of the loop only, hard direct contact over "the remainder" of the loop, with the vibration carried by that contact and not by the clearance. The disclosure affirms two things separately - that air enters beneath the rigid perimeter, and that the perimeter maintains rigid contact with the tile - but it nowhere describes where the clearance lies, that it is confined to part of the loop, that contact subsists over the balance of the loop, or that vibration crosses at the contact rather than at the gap. The broad claim recital "along at least part of the perimeter member" is the acceptable, non-exclusive reading and can stand; the description's exclusive version ('only along part ... rather than ... everywhere') is the untraced addition and is what a reader would treat as a described structural requirement.
findings.evidence: Candidate: "Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside that contact, being present only along part of the perimeter member 24 rather than separating the bearing face 26 from the exposed face 38 everywhere." Nearest source (disclosure.md): "Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter." No affirmative passage states that the clearance occupies only part of the perimeter or that contact subsists over the remainder.
findings.fix: Replace the two quoted sentences with: "Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member." This keeps literal support for the "along at least part" recital in claims 1, 10 and 14 without asserting an unsourced partition of the interface.

findings.title: Absolute "no downward force is applied by an operator" exceeds the disclosure's "without requiring the operator to press downward"
findings.where: draft/08-claims.md claim 17; draft/07-detailed-description.md "The pressure differential that holds the device down" ("In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.") and "The force balance ..." ("the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force", "Because the operator applies no downward force"); draft/05-summary.md paragraph beginning "Two consequences follow"; draft/09-abstract.md
findings.detail: The disclosure states that the pressure differential holds the device without requiring operator downward pressure, and that operator pressure and fatigue are minimized. The candidate converts a permissive statement (the operator need not press) into an absolute factual and claimed condition (the operator applies none, hands carry no part of the contact load). No affirmative passage says the operator in fact applies zero downward force or that the hands carry none of the contact load; the disclosure's own summary sentence speaks of 'minimizing' pressure, not eliminating it. Claim 17 recites the absolute as a positive method limitation, so the mismatch is a scope defect as well as a fidelity one. Claims 5 and 13 are correctly drafted ('sufficient to hold ... without a downward force being applied') and should be the model.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 17): "wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein no downward force is applied to the vibration device by an operator while the vibration motor operates." Candidate (description): "In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load." Source (disclosure.md): "The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward." and "The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator." No passage states that no downward force is applied.
findings.fix: Claim 17: replace the second clause with "and wherein the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element without a downward force being required from the operator." Description: replace "In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load." with "The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands."; replace "Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path" with "Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained"; replace "the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer" with "the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer". Abstract: change "without downward force from the operator" to "without downward force being required from the operator"; Summary: change "the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped" to "the operator need not press the device against the covering element, so the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped".

findings.title: Invented housing shapes, housing spacing and base overhang in the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs
findings.where: figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md, Geometry to be drawn (base 12, vibration motor 18, air-extraction mechanism 20, handle 44); figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md, Geometry to be drawn (vibration device 10)
findings.detail: The briefs specify shapes, proportions and spatial relationships that no source passage supplies: that the motor and the air-extraction mechanism are each a rectangular housing, that the two housings do not touch, that the motor is the left-hand housing, that the base is a flat slab that runs past both housings at both ends so that its top face is exposed beyond them, and that the handle stands clear of the two housings. The disclosure says only that the vibration motor and the air-extraction mechanism are each coupled to the first side of a rigid base, and that the device may include one or more handles. The overhang requirement in particular is an invented proportion of exactly the class the standing corrective USER message identified for removal ('remove invented exact counts and proportions not grounded in the disclosure'); it exists to create a labelling target rather than to depict a disclosed structure.
findings.evidence: Candidate (FIG. 1): "The base 12 is the flat slab that carries the other bodies, the only slab on the sheet, running past them at both ends, so that its top face is exposed beyond them." and "The vibration motor 18 is a rectangular housing standing on the top face of the base 12, drawn as the left-hand of the two housings" and "The air-extraction mechanism 20 is a rectangular housing ... the two housings not touching." Source (disclosure.md): "The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side." No affirmative passage gives any housing shape, relative position, separation, or base overhang.
findings.fix: In both briefs, recast these as depiction conventions rather than asserted structure: "The base 12 is the slab that carries the other bodies, the only slab on the sheet; its top face remains visible where no body stands on it. Identified well inside the visible part of its top face, clear of every bounding line." and "The vibration motor 18 is one of the two bodies carried on the top face of the base 12, shown as a simple housing, with no body in front of it. Identified well inside its front face." and "The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the other body carried on the top face of the base 12, shown as a separate simple housing. Identified well inside its front face." Apply the same wording to the corresponding sentence in the FIG. 5 brief ("the base, shown as a slab, and two separate simple housings carried on it").

findings.title: Rectangular plan shape of the perimeter loop is invented across FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 5

findings.title: FIG. 5 depicts a handle on the pulling-element embodiment, a combination the disclosure presents as alternatives
findings.where: figures/FIG-5-SECOND-EMBODIMENT-WITH-A-PULLING-ELEMENT.md (handle 44 bullet and "a grip carried on the assembly"); draft/06-drawings.md FIG. 5 ("the device again carrying a handle"); draft/07-detailed-description.md, "Handles" ("as shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5")
findings.detail: The disclosure introduces the handle and the flexible pulling element as separate propositions, the pulling element expressly as "another embodiment". It does not affirmatively describe a device that carries both at once. Depicting and reciting the combination in the second embodiment adds a configuration no source passage supplies. The device-level statement "may include one or more handles" is generic, but the drawing turns the combination into a specific illustrated embodiment.
findings.evidence: Candidate (FIG. 5 brief): "The handle 44 is that grip, standing clear of the two housings." and (draft/06) "FIG. 5 is a perspective view of a second embodiment in which a flexible pulling element is connected to the device ..., the device again carrying a handle." Source (disclosure.md): "The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device." No affirmative passage combines the two on one device.
findings.fix: Either (a) remove numeral 44 and the grip from the FIG. 5 brief, delete "the device again carrying a handle" from draft/06-drawings.md, and change the Detailed Description to "as shown in FIG. 1"; or (b) keep the drawing and add to the Detailed Description, "Handles" section: "The handle 44 and the flexible pulling element 46 are described independently, and a vibration device 10 may be provided with either or with both." Option (a) is the narrower, source-safest correction.

findings.title: Claim 6 conditions continuous extraction on motor operation; the description conditions it on device use
findings.where: draft/08-claims.md claim 6; draft/07-detailed-description.md, "The air-extraction mechanism" and "The pressure differential that holds the device down"
findings.detail: Claim 6 ties continuous withdrawal to the interval during which the vibration motor operates. The description ties it to the interval during which the device is in use and, elsewhere, to the interval during which the air-extraction mechanism itself runs. The disclosure states continuity of extraction without linking it to motor operation. The claim therefore recites a relationship neither the description nor the source states, and the two documents use different conditions for the same feature.
findings.evidence: Candidate (claim 6): "wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration motor operates." Candidate (description): "The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use." Source (disclosure.md): "The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere." No passage links extraction to motor operation.
findings.fix: Amend claim 6 to "wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration device is in use", matching the description verbatim.
